disclaimer: Every figure has a cited source. Current-year estimates are revised when the official consolidated numbers come out.
currentYear.basis: Both numbers are published by the ACSP, and the arithmetic between them is a multiplication: the Impostômetro closed 2025 at R$ 3,980bn (all three levels of government) and hit R$ 2 trillion at 9:09am on 27 June 2026 — 3.1% ahead of the same point in 2025, when the mark only fell on 3 July. R$ 3,980bn × 1.031 = R$ 4,103bn. The counter spreads that total across the seconds of the year; the year is not over, and the number is an estimate.
taxBurden.description: Gross tax burden of General Government in 2025: 32.40% of GDP — the highest level in the series that began in 2010.
taxBurden.previousPublished.note: The 2024 bulletin published 32.32% of GDP for that year; the 2025 bulletin revised it to 32.22%. A revision by the source, not a correction of ours — the Treasury series is restated with every edition.
taxBurdenBySphere.metric: Gross tax burden by level of government, in current R$ billions and as % of GDP
taxBurdenBySphere.scope: All three levels, on the national-accounts ruler: what the Treasury calls General Government. It is NOT the same quantity as `revenueSeries` (the Impostômetro counter, which measures cash) or `federalRevenueSeries` (the union alone, measured by the tax authority). Comparing the three with each other is comparing different rulers.
consumption.description: Approximate average share of tax embedded in consumer prices, a figure widely cited from IBPT/ACSP studies. Individual products vary a great deal (see the examples).
workDays.description: The IBPT study 'Days Worked to Pay Taxes': 149 days in 2025 (Tax Freedom Day on 29 May 2025), with 40.82% of average income going to tax.

federalRevenueDefinition.metric: Total federal revenue collected in the year, in nominal terms
federalRevenueDefinition.includes: It includes the subtotal administered by the tax authority, social security revenue and revenue administered by other agencies — the three components the tax authority itself adds up as the 'TOTAL GERAL' of the series it publishes. This ruler holds from 1995 onwards, the years marked 'completa'. 1994 is marked 'nucleo': the spreadsheet carries no social security revenue that year, and it does not compare with the rest.
federalRevenueDefinition.note: The series comes from the monthly spreadsheet the tax authority publishes itself, not from adding up the by-state file or from year-by-year news reports. The switch did three things. First, it stretched the series from thirteen years (2013-2025) to thirty-one (1995-2025) on the SAME ruler: the by-state file only carries the social security column from 2013 and the other-agencies column from 2010, and adding it up before that returns a year around 30% smaller with nothing to flag it. Second, it confirmed what was already published: where the two sources overlap (2013-2024) they agree to within 0.05%. Third, it settled the 2025 divergence — the R$ 2,886bn the tax authority announced in January 2026 is the total of its own series (R$ 2,886.9bn); what did not add up was the by-state file, which totals R$ 2,855.8bn and still serves the map, where the question is a different one.
federalRevenueDefinition.rulers.completa: The TOTAL GERAL of the tax authority's spreadsheet: administered subtotal + social security revenue + revenue administered by other agencies. It is the number the tax authority announces when the year closes.
federalRevenueDefinition.rulers.nucleo: A year in which one of the three components does not exist in the source. Today that is only 1994, which carries no social security revenue — in 1995, the first year it appears, it alone comes to R$ 35.1bn out of a R$ 119.1bn total, nearly a third. Splicing 1994 onto the rest would draw a step that is a change of definition, not of revenue.
federalRevenueDefinition.avisoParaQuemPu: The ruler comes from COUNTING THE MONTHS in which each component has a value, never from summing it: a component with a single stray month makes the sum clear zero and the year declare itself complete when it is not. That is how 2005 nearly entered as a complete ruler in the by-state file, on the strength of three months of social security revenue.
